name: Principality of Sealand
pop: Single digits at most; one permanent resident as of August 2024
currency: Sealand dollar, coins issued since 1972, nominally pegged 1:1 to the US dollar
passports: Issued from 1975; all revoked in 1997 after a Madrid-based ring sold fakes
laws: 1975 constitution; the monarch also headed the courts
challenge: Still occupied. An English court found it had no jurisdiction in 1968; a Cologne court held it was no state in 1978
recognition: None. The Bates family claims de facto recognition; the UK and Germany do not
cost: Fire damage in 2006 estimated at half a million pounds
story: Roughs Tower is a Second World War sea fort built by Britain on a sandbar about 7 nautical miles off Suffolk, then outside Britain's 3-mile territorial sea (the coastal belt a state fully controls). Roy Bates took it from Radio Caroline staff at the end of 1966 and declared the Principality of Sealand on 2 September 1967. On 6 May 1968 his son Michael fired a .22 pistol across the bow of the buoy ship Egeria. In October 1968 Mr Justice Chapman at Chelmsford ruled that Parliament had never extended the firearms law that far. In 1978 the Administrative Court of Cologne refused Alexander Achenbach's request to drop German citizenship, holding Sealand was no state. That August Achenbach's lawyer Gernot Pütz seized the platform; the Bateses retook it by helicopter on 15 August and fined Pütz 75,000 Deutsche Marks. In 1987 Britain extended its territorial sea to 12 miles, which covers the tower. A fire on 23 June 2006 sent one person to hospital by RAF helicopter. In 2007 The Pirate Bay raised over $20,000 towards buying it, and talks failed.
mechanism: R v Bates (1968) decided only that English criminal law had not been extended to the tower; Sealand reads it as recognition, while the Cologne court applied the territory, population and government test and found statehood lacking.

sources.t: Grimmelmann, Sealand, HavenCo, and the Rule of Law, University of Illinois Law Review 2012
Grimmelmann, Sealand and HavenCo Part IV: International Law and Sealand Law, The Volokh Conspiracy
Principality of Sealand, Wikipedia

name: HavenCo
founder: Sean Hastings, Jo Hastings, Ryan Lackey, Avi Freedman, Michael Bates
stopped_by: Internal dispute with the Bates family; the dot-com crash cut its network links
pop: Staff on the platform; figure not published
laws: Terms promised 'contract autonomy'; later policy banned acts against international law
challenge: Never tested by a state in court; the host platform's own rulers took control
cost: Investors hoped for a stock listing at $500 million; no amount actually raised was verified
story: HavenCo was an internet company set up to host data on Sealand, beyond the reach of other countries' courts. A place like this is called a data haven. On 22 August 2000 Michael Bates bought a dormant British company and renamed it HavenCo Limited, so the business was registered in the country it hoped to escape; it later moved its registration to Cyprus. Investors included Avi Freedman and Joichi Ito. The founders planned customers such as online casinos and subpoena-proof corporate records, and advertised first-world infrastructure with third-world regulation. Law professor James Grimmelmann found that the dot-com crash cut Sealand's network links more than any government did. Co-founder Ryan Lackey left in 2002 after disputes with the Bates family and said the company had probably been nationalized by Sealand. It could not sue, because the monarch headed Sealand's courts and any foreign court would have undercut its claim to independence. The new management banned acts against international law. The website went offline in November 2008. In 2013 Freedman announced a revival using servers in the EU and US, with some cold data on Sealand.
mechanism: HavenCo showed that a business escaping national law depends on the law of its host, here a monarchy whose ruler was also its judge, and it could not seek redress elsewhere without denying its own premise.

sources.t: Grimmelmann, Sealand, HavenCo, and the Rule of Law, University of Illinois Law Review 2012
Grimmelmann, Sealand and HavenCo Part IV: International Law and Sealand Law, The Volokh Conspiracy
HavenCo, Wikipedia

name: Knock John Tower / Radio Essex
stopped_by: UK Post Office prosecution under the Wireless Telegraphy Act
challenge: No. Convicted November 1966; appeal lost January 1967
story: Knock John is one of four naval sea forts Britain built in the Thames Estuary during the Second World War. In 1965 Roy Bates set up an unlicensed station, Radio Essex, on the fort, after driving off staff of the rival station Radio City. Grimmelmann's history gives the fort as about one and a half miles from the coast by the legal measure used, which put it inside Britain's 3-mile territorial limit. The government at first left the pirate stations alone. Enforcement rose after one radio entrepreneur shot another in June 1966. Bates received a summons on 28 September 1966 under the Wireless Telegraphy Act, which banned unlicensed broadcasting. Government files recorded interference as far away as Hungary. On 30 November magistrates found him guilty and fined him £100. His appeal failed in January 1967. By then he had shut down on Christmas Day 1966 and moved to Roughs Tower, farther out, which he would soon declare to be Sealand. The Post Office was still pursuing him for the costs of his appeal months later.
mechanism: The case turned on measuring the 3-mile limit, and the loss pushed Bates to a fort beyond it, the direct origin of Sealand's jurisdiction argument.

sources.t: Grimmelmann, Sealand, HavenCo, and the Rule of Law, University of Illinois Law Review 2012
Maunsell Forts (Knock John Tower), Wikipedia

name: Radio 390 / Red Sands Fort
aka: R v Kent Justices ex parte Lye
stopped_by: UK courts and the Marine Broadcasting Offences Act 1967
challenge: No. Convicted 1966 and 1967, enjoined, then outlawed
cost: Fines: £100 in 1966; £200 plus £40 per director in 1967
story: Radio 390 broadcast easy-listening programmes from Red Sands, an abandoned army fort in the Thames Estuary, after two weak earlier stations on the site failed in 1965. Everything depended on whether the fort lay outside Britain's 3-mile territorial limit. On 25 November 1966 a magistrates' court convicted the station's managers of illegal broadcasting and fined them £100. The High Court rejected the appeal in December, in the case R v Kent Justices ex parte Lye, holding 2 to 1 that the fort was inside the limit because the distance could be measured from a low-tide elevation, meaning a sandbank that shows only at low water, as set by a 1964 Order in Council. The station returned on 31 December with fresh evidence on the fort's position. Magistrates rejected that in February 1967 and fined the company £200 and its directors £40 each. The Post Office won a civil injunction in May. An appeal was refused on 28 July because the new Marine Broadcasting Offences Act would close the station by 14 August anyway. It went off the air that day.
mechanism: R v Kent Justices held that a low-tide sandbank can move the baseline for the territorial sea outward, which brought an offshore fort inside national jurisdiction.

sources.t: Grimmelmann, Sealand, HavenCo, and the Rule of Law, University of Illinois Law Review 2012
Radio 390, Wikipedia

name: Radio City / Shivering Sands Fort
founder: Screaming Lord Sutch; later Reginald Calvert
challenge: No
story: Radio City began as Radio Sutch on 27 May 1964, broadcasting from the abandoned Shivering Sands army fort in the Thames Estuary. It was founded by the musician Screaming Lord Sutch and later owned by Reginald Calvert. In June 1966 Calvert's sale talks with a group led by Major Oliver Smedley, behind Radio Atlanta, broke down, with a dispute over a transmitter Smedley had supplied. At 3 a.m. on 20 June seamen sent by Smedley boarded the fort and took it from the disc jockeys. The next evening Calvert went to Smedley's home and was shot dead there. Smedley was charged with murder and cleared on grounds of self-defence. Grimmelmann's history records that this heavily reported shooting shifted public feeling and led the government to step up enforcement of the Wireless Telegraphy Act against the offshore stations, including Roy Bates's Radio Essex. Radio City made its last broadcast on 8 February 1967.
mechanism: The killing over a fort no one clearly policed became the political trigger for enforcing broadcasting law against the sea forts.

sources.t: Grimmelmann, Sealand, HavenCo, and the Rule of Law, University of Illinois Law Review 2012
Radio City (pirate radio station), Wikipedia

name: Radio Caroline and the pirate radio ships
stopped_by: Marine, &c., Broadcasting (Offences) Act 1967, which cut off British support
challenge: Partly. Kept broadcasting from international waters after 1967, but British subjects could no longer associate with it
story: In 1964 Ronan O'Rahilly fitted out a ship, MV Caroline, as a radio station and anchored it off Felixstowe, Suffolk, to break the BBC's monopoly on British radio. Its first programme went out on 28 March 1964. A second ship, MV Mi Amigo, sat off Frinton-on-Sea as Radio Caroline South. Because a ship in international waters falls outside a coastal state's territorial sea, the station needed no British licence. Other offshore stations came before it, including Radio Mercur, aimed at Denmark from 1958, and Radio Veronica, aimed at the Netherlands from 1960. Governments answered with an international treaty, the European Agreement for the Prevention of Broadcasts Transmitted from Stations outside National Territories. Britain put it into law through the Marine, &c., Broadcasting (Offences) Act 1967, which received royal assent on 14 July and took effect on 15 August 1967. The Act did not reach the ship. It made it illegal for a British subject to associate with such a station. Caroline carried on using five ships in turn until 1990.
mechanism: Unable to reach a ship broadcasting from international waters, Britain regulated its own subjects, which avoided deciding who governed the vessel.

Marine, &c., Broadcasting (Offences) Act 1967, Wikipedia
REM Island, Wikipedia

name: Republic of Rose Island
stopped_by: Italian police and navy; Italian Council of State
pop: A guard and his partner when police arrived
currency: The mill, on stamps; no coins or notes are known
laws: Declared a republic with its own government; official language Esperanto
challenge: No. Seized after 55 days and demolished; Council of State rejected the sovereignty claim
story: Bologna engineer Giorgio Rosa conceived the platform in 1958, placing it nearly 12 kilometres off Rimini, a few hundred metres outside Italian territorial waters. It was a 400-square-metre deck on nine pylons. Late in 1966 the Rimini harbour office asked him to stop work, partly because nearby areas were leased to the state energy company ENI. He continued and opened to visitors in summer 1967, with a bar, restaurant, nightclub, shop and post office. On 1 May 1968 he declared independence, with himself as president and Esperanto as the language. Italian officials suspected a way to avoid tax on tourist income. On 26 June police and tax officers took control and set a blockade; only the guard and his partner were aboard. Rosa telegraphed President Saragat and got no reply. In August the merchant marine ministry ordered demolition, and his appeal failed. The platform survived two explosive charges in February 1969, and a storm sank it on 26 February. The Council of State, Italy's top administrative court, then held the claims of independence unfounded and said Italian citizens stay subject to Italian law abroad.
mechanism: The Council of State reasoned from the builder's nationality: a citizen's platform outside territorial waters stays under his country's law, whatever he declares.

sources.t: La storia dell'Isola delle Rose, Il Post, 29 Aug 2012
Republic of Rose Island, Wikipedia

name: REM Island / TV Noordzee
stopped_by: Dutch Parliament's anti-REM law and Dutch marines
challenge: No. Boarded five days after a new law was passed
story: In the early 1960s the Netherlands had one television channel, shared among public broadcasters, and advertising was banned. A company called REM built a platform in the harbour of Cork, Ireland, towed it to a spot 10 kilometres off Noordwijk and fixed it to the seabed in cement. It was the first European pirate station on a purpose-built structure, where earlier ones used ships. Test broadcasts began on 15 August 1964, and TV Noordzee started regular shows on 1 September, with Dutch and foreign advertising and imported American and British series. It targeted about 750,000 television sets. Dutch law banned such broadcasts, but the platform stood outside territorial waters, so officials had no power to act. On 12 December 1964 the government passed a law dividing the North Sea into continental sections, declaring the seabed under the structure Dutch territory. Five days later Dutch marines boarded the platform and ended transmissions. A year later the company's successor resumed legally as the public broadcaster TROS. The government later used the platform to measure sea temperature. It was dismantled in 2006 and became a restaurant in Amsterdam in 2011.
mechanism: The Dutch state reached a structure beyond its territorial sea by claiming the seabed it stood on, so any platform fixed to the continental shelf falls under the coastal state.

sources.t: REM Island, Wikipedia
TV Noordzee, Wikipedia

name: Republic of Minerva
founder: Michael Oliver; provisional president Morris C. 'Bud' Davis
stopped_by: King Taufa'ahau Tupou IV of Tonga
currency: Minerva dollar coins, including a 35-dollar piece
laws: Promised no taxation, welfare or subsidies; Oliver had published a constitution for a new country in 1968
challenge: No. Tonga removed it within months
recognition: None; Tonga's claim was recognised by the South Pacific Forum
cost: About 2,000 investors backed the foundation; total not verified
story: Nevada real estate developer and coin dealer Michael Oliver raised money from about 2,000 investors through the Ocean Life Research Foundation. He first tried to buy an island from a government and found no seller. In 1971 barges brought sand from Australia and piled it on the Minerva Reefs, which were submerged at high tide, adding a small platform and flag. A declaration of independence went to neighbouring states on 19 January 1972. Tonga had not included the reefs in its 1887 territorial claim. Fiji's prime minister asked what would stop such people claiming land in Fiji. At a conference on 24 February, Australia, New Zealand, Fiji, Nauru, Samoa and the Cook Islands backed Tonga's claim. A Tongan proclamation of 15 June claimed the reefs and waters within 12 miles. A Tongan expedition arrived on 18 June, and the Tongan flag went up on North Minerva on 19 June and South Minerva on 21 June. The king sailed with a convict work detail and a four-piece brass band, and the platform was dismantled within hours. Oliver then dismissed Davis and the project collapsed.
mechanism: Nearby states responded to a private artificial island on an unclaimed reef by agreeing that one of them should annex it, which closed the gap the founders relied on.

sources.t: Republic of Minerva, Wikipedia
Pendle, New Foundlands, Cabinet, Summer 2005
The Libertarian Dream Was Tried Here, History News Network
Craib, The Brief Life and Watery Death of a '70s Libertarian Micronation (Slate excerpt, PM Press)

name: Minerva Reefs: 1982 reoccupation and Fiji-Tonga dispute
stopped_by: Tongan troops
pop: A small American group for three weeks
challenge: No. Removed after three weeks
story: Ten years after Tonga annexed the Minerva Reefs, a group of Americans led by Morris C. 'Bud' Davis, the Republic of Minerva's former provisional president, tried to occupy them again in 1982. Tongan troops forced them off after three weeks. The sources found for this research report no group taking possession since then, and Reason magazine later described the structure as more or less reclaimed by the sea. The state-to-state argument outlasted the private claim. In 2005 Fiji declared that it did not recognise any maritime claims by Tonga based on the reefs under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, the 1982 treaty that sets out how far states' rights extend at sea. In November 2005 Fiji lodged a complaint with the International Seabed Authority about Tonga's claims, and Tonga lodged a counter-claim. The reefs are two submerged atolls lying between the two countries. The stakes are the rights over surrounding waters that a recognised feature can generate.
mechanism: A private claim on a reef was ended by force, but the annexation it provoked left a live dispute between two states over which maritime rights the reef generates.

sources.t: Republic of Minerva, Wikipedia
Minerva Reefs, Wikipedia

name: Abaco Independence Movement
founder: Chuck Hall and Bert Williams, funded by Michael Oliver's Phoenix Foundation
stopped_by: Loss of credibility after links to mercenary Mitchell WerBell; dissolved 1977
pop: Existing island residents; no new settlement
laws: Draft constitution for an Abaco Commonwealth, published 1975
challenge: No armed test; no one was arrested or charged over an insurrection
story: Abaco is an inhabited island chain in the Bahamas, included here because the money came from the same backer as the Minerva reef project. As Bahamian independence approached in 1973, some white residents objected to living under black rule. Chuck Hall and Bert Williams founded the Abaco Independence Movement in August 1973, and Michael Oliver's Phoenix Foundation agreed to fund it. The movement proposed placing all Crown land in a trust, giving each citizen a one-acre lot and a share of land revenue, and developing a 60-square-mile free trade zone. Its first convention, on 23 February 1974, was addressed by John Hospers, the US Libertarian Party's 1972 presidential candidate, who was later refused entry to the Bahamas. In February 1975 Esquire magazine reported that a rising was being planned, and American arms dealer Mitchell WerBell said Abaco would declare independence unilaterally. No arrests followed, but the WerBell connection damaged the group. In March 1975 it renamed itself the Abaco Home Rule Movement, denied military aims and published a draft constitution. It dissolved in 1977.
mechanism: Foreign libertarian financing tried to detach an inhabited territory at the moment of a state's decolonization, in place of building new land at sea.

sources.t: Abaco Independence Movement, Wikipedia
Phoenix Foundation, Wikipedia

name: Republic of Vemerana
founder: Jimmy Stevens, funded by Michael Oliver's Phoenix Foundation
stopped_by: Government of Vanuatu with Papua New Guinea troops
challenge: No. Revolt crushed in August 1980; Stevens jailed
cost: US$250,000 from the Phoenix Foundation to Stevens and Nagriamel, as revealed at his trial
story: Espiritu Santo is an island in Vanuatu, formerly the New Hebrides. Jimmy Stevens led Nagriamel, a conservative movement there, and the allied New Hebrides Autonomy Movement had lost recent elections. In 1980 he declared the island the independent State of Vemerana, in alliance with Michael Oliver of the Phoenix Foundation, the libertarian group already behind the Minerva and Abaco attempts. Vanuatu's government asked Papua New Guinea for help, and Papua New Guinea sent a battalion of soldiers. The revolt was crushed in August 1980. At Stevens's trial it emerged that he and Nagriamel had received US$250,000 from the Phoenix Foundation. One allegation, reported by a third-world research institute and marked uncited in the encyclopedia entry, was that the money also bought arms, a radio and casino concessions; it is unverified here. Stevens was convicted and sentenced to 14 years. He escaped on 12 September 1982, was recaptured two days later, and was freed on 14 August 1991. He died on 28 February 1994. The case is on land and is included for its link to the ocean projects.
mechanism: A new state used foreign military help to end a privately funded secession, showing that recognised governments can call on one another against such claims.

sources.t: Jimmy Stevens (politician), Wikipedia
Phoenix Foundation, Wikipedia

name: Operation Atlantis
stopped_by: Gunboats at Silver Shoals; hurricanes; Haitian government
pop: A small group at a New York motel; no verified figure
currency: The deca, holding a decagram of silver, struck on a soap press
laws: Constitution drafted by Spencer Heath MacCallum for a 2% share
challenge: No. Ordered off Silver Shoals and expelled from Tortuga
cost: Stiefel agreed $100,000 for the Prickly Pear Cays; sale did not complete
story: Werner Stiefel, head of a soap and dermatology company, started Operation Atlantis in 1968 at a motel in Saugerties, New York, inspired by Ayn Rand. He tried to buy the Prickly Pear Cays near Anguilla for $100,000, and the sale fell through. Members spent a year building a 38-foot ferro-cement boat, Atlantis II, under a geodesic dome. Launched on the Hudson River in December 1971, it capsized at low tide. It later reached the Bahamas, where a storm destroyed it. Stiefel bought another ship and went to Silver Shoals, an area claimed by both Haiti and the Bahamas, with water four feet deep at low tide. He built sea walls and was about to dredge sand when gunboats ordered his group to leave; accounts differ on whether they were Haitian or Dominican. He then leased a base on Tortuga, Haiti, until officials read the group's newsletter and cancelled the lease. An oil rig bound for the Misteriosa Bank was destroyed by a hurricane. A participant says the group later bought Hatchet Caye in Belize and lived there until 2005.
mechanism: An unmarked shoal claimed by two nearby states offered no real legal vacuum, because a coastal navy could remove an unarmed group without any court being involved.

sources.t: Simpson, Operation Atlantis: A case-study in libertarian island micronationality, Shima 10(2), 2016
Operation Atlantis, Wikipedia
Craib, The Brief Life and Watery Death of a '70s Libertarian Micronation (Slate excerpt, PM Press)
Silver Bank (coordinates), Wikipedia

name: Abalonia
stopped_by: Ocean waves destroyed the ship; the US later declared the bank continental shelf
laws: Planned as a constitutional monarchy
challenge: Physically ended before any state acted
story: Cortes Bank is a shallow seamount about 100 miles from San Diego, topped by Bishop Rock in very shallow water. In 1966 a team of entrepreneurs planned to turn it into a constitutional monarchy called Abalonia. A newspaper story of 31 October 1966, 'Pair Planning Island Nation off San Diego', first reported it. The plan was to scuttle a Second World War concrete-hulled freighter, the SS Jalisco, on Bishop Rock, then surround it with a growing ring of boulders and use it as a seafood processing plant. The group reasoned that because the bank lay in international waters, maritime law would let them rule their own nation. The ship was towed out under San Francisco's Bay Bridge. Waves broke it apart on the rock and the crew were nearly killed. Jim Houtz, who was aboard and was injured, later told writer Chris Dixon the affair cost him his marriage and led to financial ruin. The wreck lies in three pieces in 6 to 40 feet of water. When another company later proposed a nation called Taluga there, the US government declared the bank US territory as part of the continental shelf.
mechanism: The US answered later proposals on the bank by treating a shallow seamount as part of its continental shelf, a rule that also defeated similar plans off Florida.

sources.t: Cortes Bank, Wikipedia
Dixon, A Conversation With the King of Abalonia, The Inertia, 2011
Grimmelmann, Sealand, HavenCo, and the Rule of Law, University of Illinois Law Review 2012

name: Principality of New Utopia
founder: Howard Turney, known as Lazarus Long
stopped_by: US Securities and Exchange Commission; federal judge Michael Burrage
currency: Paper currency showing Long's face, per the SEC
laws: Planned 20% tax on imported goods
challenge: No. Assets frozen April 1999; consent judgment January 2000
cost: SEC found $24,000 raised against a $350 million bond offer; AP reported an early estimate near $100,000
story: Howard Turney, who ran an anti-ageing clinic in Mexico, renamed himself Lazarus Long around 1995 after a character in Robert Heinlein's novels. He promoted New Utopia, a tax-free country on concrete platforms over the Misteriosa Bank, an underwater rise about 115 miles west of the Cayman Islands. A website of more than 100 pages offered government bonds at 9.5 percent and promised currency returns as high as 200 percent. Plans included 642 apartments and a casino. On 8 April 1999 the US Securities and Exchange Commission filed suit, alleging false statements about construction, the companies involved, the safety of the investment and the agency's own inquiry. Judge Michael Burrage in Tulsa issued an emergency order freezing the money. The AP put it near $100,000 at that stage. On 20 January 2000 Long accepted a final judgment without contesting it, and was barred from further violations. The $24,000 repayment and interest were waived because he swore he could not pay. Encyclopedia claims of $100 million raised conflict with the SEC's figure. He died in April 2012. His daughter announced a revival in 2017, with no later updates found.
mechanism: US securities law applied to internet sales aimed at US investors whatever flag or territory the offer claimed, so a sovereignty story gave no shelter from fraud rules.

sources.t: SEC Litigation Release No. 16425, Lazarus R. Long
AP, SEC says New Utopia offer is just another Web scam, Deseret News, 11 Apr 1999
New Utopia, Wikipedia

name: Grand Capri Republic and Atlantis, Isle of Gold
founder: Louis M. Ray and Acme General Contractors; Atlantis Development Corporation
stopped_by: US Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit
challenge: No. Permanently barred by federal injunction
story: Triumph and Long Reefs are two coral reefs about four and a half miles off southeast Florida near Miami, submerged except for brief exposure at low tide. They lay in international waters at the time. Louis M. Ray and Acme General Contractors planned a new nation there called Grand Capri Republic. They placed caissons, large watertight boxes, on the reefs and filled them with dredged seabed material. A rival, Atlantis Development Corporation, claimed better title through an earlier discovery and planned a country called Atlantis, Isle of Gold, with commercial buildings on pilings. On 16 November 1964 Acme applied to the Army Corps of Engineers to build a 20-acre resort island, and the Corps refused. Ray dredged anyway. The trial court granted a preliminary injunction on 21 April 1965. In January 1969 it barred construction but rejected the trespass count, because the government did not own the reefs. In 1970 the Fifth Circuit held that the reefs were seabed of the outer continental shelf, where the US holds exclusive rights to explore and exploit resources under the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act and the Geneva Convention on the Continental Shelf. It ordered a full permanent injunction, noting harm to corals and to shipping.
mechanism: United States v. Ray (1970) held that a coastal state can stop building on its continental shelf without owning the seabed, because its exclusive resource rights support an injunction.

sources.t: United States v. Ray, 423 F.2d 16 (5th Cir. 1970), Justia
United States v. Ray, 294 F. Supp. 532 (S.D. Fla. 1969), Leagle
United States v. Ray, 281 F. Supp. 876 (S.D. Fla. 1965), Justia

name: Principality of Trinidad
stopped_by: Britain's 1895 landing, then Brazilian diplomacy
laws: Self-proclaimed military dictatorship planned; created a chivalric order
challenge: No. Britain occupied it in 1895 and Brazil's claim prevailed
cost: Sold government bonds; amount not verified
story: Trindade is a small uninhabited island in the South Atlantic. James Harden-Hickey, a Franco-American writer and duellist, saw it on a voyage and treated it as terra nullius, meaning land belonging to no one. In 1893 he proclaimed himself James I, Prince of Trinidad. He designed stamps, a flag and a coat of arms, founded an order called the Cross of Trinidad, bought a schooner for colonists, named a Secretary of State and opened a consular office at 217 West 36th Street in New York. He issued bonds to pay for building on the island. In 1895 The New York Times reported that the British warship Barracouta had taken possession while he was in California. Britain based its claim on a 1700 visit by Edmund Halley and wanted the island for a telegraph cable station. Harden-Hickey appealed to Washington. Brazil pressed its own claim from Portuguese discovery in 1502 and won. The state of Espírito Santo built a marker on 24 January 1897, and Brazil keeps a navy post there. Harden-Hickey died in El Paso, Texas, on 9 February 1898.
mechanism: A private claim based on terra nullius collapsed once established states contested the island, and the outcome turned on old discovery claims argued between governments.

sources.t: Principality of Trinidad, Wikipedia
James Harden-Hickey, Wikipedia

name: Republic of Morac-Songhrati-Meads
stopped_by: Ignored by states; no enforcement needed
challenge: Never tested; a 1985 lawsuit for $25 billion was not heard
recognition: None; UN, China and Philippines petitioned in 1972 without result
story: This claim covers the Spratly Islands, a disputed group of reefs and islets in the South China Sea. Claimants traced it to a British sea captain, James George Meads, said to have claimed the islands in 1877 and called himself King James I. A rival body called the Kingdom of Humanity is said to date from 1914. The first verifiable evidence comes only from 1946, when Morton F. Meads, an American soldier, was discharged in Manila for private business in army surplus. Philippine newspapers repeated his stories of a family birthright, and they drew the attention of businessmen such as Tomás Cloma, who then raced to claim the islands. The entities' real activity was limited to items such as postage stamps; stamps from 1959 are known. Meads petitioned the UN, the Republic of China and the Philippines in 1972 and was unsuccessful. That year, the account goes, the rest of the governing body drowned in a shipwreck during Typhoon Ora. In 1985 he sued the United States and others for $25 billion, and the case was not heard. Descendants were still asserting a claim in the 1990s.
mechanism: An undocumented family claim with no occupation carried no weight, though it reportedly spurred a rival private claim that later fed into a state's sovereignty argument.

sources.t: Republic of Morac-Songhrati-Meads, Wikipedia

name: Free Territory of Freedomland
stopped_by: Republic of China navy; President Ferdinand Marcos of the Philippines
pop: A 40-man expedition; no lasting civil population verified
laws: Government named 1956, capital on Flat Island; new constitution drafted August 1974
challenge: No. Taiwan burned buildings in 1956; Cloma signed his rights to the Philippines in 1974
recognition: None; the Philippines later absorbed the claim
cost: Rights signed over to the Philippines for one peso in 1974
story: Tomás Cloma owned a fishing fleet and a maritime school in the Philippines. His brother Filemon reportedly found the area when a typhoon pushed his boats west of Palawan in 1947. On 11 May 1956 Filemon led 40 men in taking formal possession of 53 islands and islets some 380 miles west of Palawan, and posted a 'Notice to the Whole World'. Tomás argued the area had no owner because Japan had given it up at San Francisco in 1951. He declared the Free Territory of Freedomland on 21 May, with a capital on Flat Island from July. On 1 October 1956 at North Danger Reef, Taiwanese naval ships met Filemon's boat, and Taiwan later burned buildings and took property. The brothers then asked the Philippine government for support. In 1972 Marcos jailed Tomás for four months for impersonating an officer by using the title admiral. In August 1974 the group adopted a new constitution and renamed the territory Colonia. In December 1974 Tomás was arrested and made to convey his rights to the Philippines for one peso. A 1978 decree made the area the Municipality of Kalayaan.
mechanism: A private claim to unowned land turned into a state's title: the Philippines cites the forced 1974 transfer as one basis for its claim, showing how states can absorb and reuse private occupation.

sources.t: Free Territory of Freedomland, Wikipedia

name: Global State of Waveland
pop: Three to four Greenpeace activists for 42 days
passports: Citizenship offered to anyone taking a pledge of allegiance
challenge: Not challenged by force; Britain said anyone may go there and stay
recognition: None; a recognition petition to Britain was not accepted
story: Rockall is a small rock in the North Atlantic, about 301 kilometres from the nearest land in Scotland. Britain claimed it in 1955 and made it part of Scotland in 1972. Ireland, Iceland and Denmark have contested the rights around it, because whoever holds it might claim surrounding seabed where oil may lie. In June 1997 Greenpeace activists landed to protest oil exploration in the Atlantic, including BP's £1 billion Foinhaven field. They stayed 42 days, then a record. They declared the rock the capital of the Global State of Waveland and offered citizenship to anyone willing to take a pledge of allegiance. Flag records say Prime Minister Tony Blair refused their petition for recognition. The British government said Rockall was British territory, part of Scotland, and that anyone was free to go there and stay as long as they pleased. John Vidal, one of the three, said the team unscrewed the 1955 British plaque and refixed it back to front. Greenpeace returned for a second landing in 1998. The occupation served as a launch point for actions against seismic survey ships and rigs.
mechanism: Greenpeace used a contested rock's legal uncertainty for protest, and Britain's answer treated the occupiers as visitors on British soil, giving the claim nothing to push against.

name: Tom McClean's occupation of Rockall
recognition: Not a claim of independence; meant to support Britain's claim
story: Tom McClean, a Dublin-born adventurer and veteran of the Parachute Regiment and the Special Air Service, lived on Rockall from 26 May to 4 July 1985, in what one account calls a wooden box. His stated purpose ran opposite to a breakaway state: he wanted to strengthen Britain's claim to the rock. Britain had claimed Rockall in 1955 and incorporated it into Scotland in 1972, and it claims a 12-nautical-mile territorial sea around it. Ireland has never claimed sovereignty but disputes Britain's position. The 40-day stay set a record for solo occupation. Greenpeace beat the total in 1997 with 42 days, and Nick Hancock reached 45 days alone in 2014 after a storm took some of his supplies. The encyclopedia entry on McClean flags as doubtful the statement that his stay reaffirmed Britain's claim. Under the 1982 UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, a rock that cannot sustain human habitation or economic life has no exclusive economic zone or continental shelf of its own, which is why people's ability to live there has been of interest.
mechanism: McClean's stay tested the idea that personal occupation could support a state's claim to a rock whose capacity for human life bears on the maritime rights it generates.

name: Gay and Lesbian Kingdom of the Coral Sea Islands
stopped_by: Dissolved by its own leaders after Australia's 2017 marriage vote
pop: No one lived there; a campsite was the claimed capital
passports: Anyone gay or lesbian could qualify for residence and citizenship
laws: Anderson 'elected' administrator and declared emperor; national anthem 'I Am What I Am'
challenge: No state challenge found; the islands remained an Australian territory
story: The Coral Sea Islands are an uninhabited Australian external territory of small islands and reefs east of the Great Barrier Reef. In May 2004 the Australian government brought a bill to Parliament that defined marriage as between a man and a woman. On 14 June 2004 activists led by Dale Parker Anderson raised the rainbow flag on Cato Island, the territory's highest point, and claimed the islands as a homeland for gay and lesbian people. A plaque there records the date. A campsite called Heaven was named the capital. In a scheme modelled on Israel's Law of Return, any gay or lesbian person could gain permanent residence and be eligible for citizenship. Anderson was elected administrator and then declared emperor. Scholar Judy Lattas of Macquarie University, who interviewed him in 2007, treats it as a secession and argues that gay nationalism may need territorial claims to secure rights. The encyclopedia entry calls it a symbolic protest. The Kingdom was dissolved on 17 November 2017, after the 'Yes' result in Australia's postal survey on same-sex marriage.
mechanism: This was a claim inside undisputed state territory, used as protest: it borrowed the form of secession to press for equal marriage law, and ended when the law's direction changed.

name: Freedom Ship
stopped_by: Lack of financing
cost: US$6 billion estimated in 1999; US$11 billion by 2002; US$10 billion in 2013; up to US$20 billion by 2026
story: Freedom Ship is a floating city proposed in the late 1990s by engineer Norman Nixon. The name reflects the aim of a mobile colony free of the property, municipal and federal laws of any state. The plan was a chain of linked barges 1,800 metres long and 250 metres wide, with 25 floors and homes for about 80,000 people, plus a hospital, schools, hotel, casino and duty-free shops. It would constantly circle the globe, stopping at ports. For comparison, the largest ship ever built, the Seawise Giant, was about a quarter of that length. Freedom Ship International estimated the net cost at US$6 billion in 1999 and US$11 billion by 2002. A July 2008 press release explained the difficulty of finding reliable funding. In November 2013 the company said the project was being revived at US$10 billion, with construction not yet begun. In 2016 it was linked to Kanethara Marine in India. By 2026 estimates had reached US$15 billion and then US$20 billion. The project has no fixed site, so the map marker is a placeholder in mid-Atlantic.
mechanism: Freedom Ship relies on the idea that a constantly moving vessel escapes tax and property law, an idea untested because the ship was never financed.

sources.t: Freedom Ship, Wikipedia

name: The Seasteading Institute
pop: No one lives on an institute seastead
cost: Peter Thiel gave $500,000 in initial seed money
story: The Seasteading Institute is a US non-profit founded by Wayne Gramlich and Patri Friedman on 15 April 2008. A seastead is a permanent home at sea. The founders pointed out that under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, a state's exclusive economic zone, where it controls resources, runs 200 nautical miles from shore, and beyond it the high seas fall under no state's law apart from a ship's flag state. PayPal co-founder Peter Thiel gave $500,000. In 2008 they hoped to float a prototype in San Francisco Bay by 2010 and a seastead by 2014, and they met neither target. In January 2009 the institute patented ClubStead, a design for a 200-person resort seastead about the size of a city block. In July 2009 Friedman launched Ephemerisle, a floating gathering in the Sacramento-San Joaquin River Delta, inside California, which continued without him. A conference in October 2008 drew 45 people from nine countries. The institute later moved toward working inside a state's waters, as in French Polynesia. It was still publishing in 2024, promoting safety standards after the death of Samuele Landi.
mechanism: The institute's premise is that the high seas beyond 200 miles offer a place for new governance, subject only to a flag state; its own first real deal instead sought permission from a government.

name: Floating Island Project, French Polynesia
founder: The Seasteading Institute; Blue Frontiers; Randolph Hencken
stopped_by: French Polynesian government, after local opposition
laws: Planned 'special governing framework' in an 'innovative special economic zone'
challenge: No court test; government called the agreement void
recognition: French Polynesia signed a non-binding memorandum, later declared void
story: In January 2017 French Polynesia signed a memorandum of understanding with the US-based Seasteading Institute in San Francisco. Minister Jean-Christophe Bouissou signed for the territory and executive director Randolph Hencken for the institute, with President Edouard Fritch appearing by video. A memorandum records intentions and is usually weaker than a contract. The deal cleared the way for feasibility studies toward a legal structure for 'seazones' with a special governing framework, and the institute formed a company, Blue Frontiers, to build the project. It chose the territory for its links to France, its autonomy and its calm waters. The institute had inspected sites near Tahiti, Tupai and Raiatea, and the Atimaono lagoon south of Tahiti was considered for its depth and closeness to shore. Local residents objected. Opposition politician Valentina Cross held up a protest poster and asked the government to withdraw. The ruling Tapura Huiraatira party first said nothing had been signed. On 28 February 2018 RNZ reported the government's position: the deal had no legal force, had expired at the end of 2017, and was now void.
mechanism: Working within a state's waters meant any special legal zone depended on political consent, which local opposition and a non-binding document could withdraw at no cost to the government.

name: XLII Seastead off Phuket
founder: Ocean Builders; Chad Elwartowski and Supranee Thepdet
stopped_by: Royal Thai Navy
pop: Two people for about two months
laws: Occupants announced autonomy beyond any country's courts
challenge: No. Raided and towed away; occupants charged under a law carrying death or life in prison
story: Bitcoin trader Chad Elwartowski, 46, and his Thai partner Supranee Thepdet lived in a six-metre-wide cabin raised on a weighted spar, 14 nautical miles off Phuket. Ocean Builders paid for and built it, and the Seasteading Institute says it was set up on 2 February 2019 and called XLII. Elwartowski said 20 more would go on sale to form a community. They left before the Thai navy raided it on 13 April 2019. Thailand revoked his visa and charged them under a law on violating sovereignty, which carries life in prison or death. Rear Admiral Vithanarat Kochaseni said they had announced autonomy beyond any courts and invited others to join. On 22 April three navy boats began towing the cabin to shore as evidence. Ocean Builders said it sat in the contiguous zone, 12 to 24 miles out, where few Thai rules apply, and that no micronation was intended. Thailand said it sat in its 200-mile exclusive economic zone, the belt where a coastal state controls resources. In July 2019 prosecutors said nine more suspects would be charged. The outcome of the case was not found.
mechanism: The case tests whether a coastal state can treat a private structure in its exclusive economic zone as a crime against its sovereignty, far past the 12-mile line of full territorial control.

name: MS Satoshi
stopped_by: Marine insurers; no protection and indemnity cover was available
challenge: Failed before any state challenge
story: Ocean Builders announced in early October 2020 that it would turn a 1991 cruise ship, P&O's Pacific Dawn, into a floating community renamed Satoshi, anchored full-time in the Gulf of Panama. It took delivery on 5 November. Staterooms were to be auctioned as homes for entrepreneurs, digital nomads and cryptocurrency companies, with first residents expected as early as January 2021. CEO Grant Romundt told investors the project could not go on because no protection and indemnity insurer would cover it. That is the liability cover a ship's owners need against claims at sea. Without it there could be no crew, which meant losing the ship's class rating and flag, and with them any right to run businesses on board. He wrote that assuming it would be easy to insure a stationary residential ship had been incorrect. The ship was sold for scrap on 18 December 2020 and was to continue to India. Trade press later reported it had been arrested in Panama, meaning held by court order, then released and sold to a new cruise startup in 2021.
mechanism: Satoshi showed that a ship's legal life depends on private insurers: no insurance meant no crew, no class rating and no flag, and so no lawful status at sea.

name: SeaPods, Panama
pop: Overnight guests from 2023; resident count not verified
laws: Sited at a marina in Colón, Panama
challenge: Not challenged; operates inside Panama
story: After leaving Thailand and giving up on the Satoshi, Ocean Builders turned to floating homes built inside a state's waters. In September 2022 Panamanian newspaper Panamá América reported the houses being built at Linton Bay Marina in Colón, designed with Dutch architect Koen Olthuis and his firm Waterstudio. The company took reservations for a $100 deposit and said its goal was SeaPods in every corner of the ocean. A SeaPod floats on the water's surface, tethered to the seabed with anchors. It runs mainly on solar power, collects rain water and carries Starlink internet and more than 100 sensors. By June 2023 a Condé Nast Traveler writer stayed in one off Panama's Caribbean coast as among the first guests. A researcher with the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute told the writer that floating pods touch the seabed less than bungalows on pillars. Nothing found claims independence from Panama. This research did not verify later resident numbers, so the status reflects the most recent reports found.
mechanism: After the Thai raid, the same promoters sited their homes in a host state's marina, accepting national jurisdiction in place of testing the limits of the sea.

name: Blueseed
founder: Max Marty, Dario Mutabdzija, Dan Dascalescu
stopped_by: Lack of funding
challenge: Not tested
cost: US$300,000 seed funding reported; launch needed $18 million more
story: Blueseed was a Palo Alto startup, founded on 31 July 2011, that planned to house startup founders on a ship anchored 12 nautical miles off the California coast near Silicon Valley. That spot lies just outside the US territorial sea, in the contiguous zone, where a coastal state has only limited powers. The point was US immigration law. Foreign entrepreneurs could work on the ship without an H-1B work visa, and travel to the mainland on easier business or tourist visas. The project received wide press coverage and a promised investment from Peter Thiel, who ultimately did not invest in the seed round. It reported US$300,000 in seed funding, some Bitcoin investments and $9 million from an undisclosed investor, and said it would lease a ship. Its launch date moved from the third quarter of 2013 to late 2014, on the assumption that $18 million more would come in. The money did not arrive and the project went on hold in 2013. The encyclopedia entry says the company later resumed in 2020 as an accelerator and dropped the ship plan.
mechanism: Blueseed aimed to use the 12-mile line to separate where people work from where work visas are required, a plan never tested because the ship was never leased.

sources.t: Blueseed, Wikipedia

name: Life at Sea Cruises
stopped_by: The company had no ship
challenge: Not tested
cost: Cruises costing up to hundreds of thousands of dollars; 111 cabins sold; refunds promised
story: Life at Sea Cruises sold a three-year round-the-world voyage in which passengers would live aboard at prices the company said rivalled ordinary living costs. It was due to leave Istanbul, Turkey, on 1 November 2023. Shortly before that, the date moved to 11 November and the port to Amsterdam, and then to 30 November. On 17 November passengers were told the cruise was off, and the company admitted it had no ship. Some of the buyers of the 111 cabins sold were already in Istanbul. Others said they had sold or let their homes and given away their possessions. Most had spent tens of thousands of dollars. The company promised to repay in monthly instalments from mid-December to late February and offered to pay for flights home and hotels until 1 December. The case involved no claim of sovereignty. It is included as a contrast with Villa Vie and The World: it shows what buyers risked when they paid a private company for a home at sea before any ship existed. A former executive said she was not speaking for the parent company, Miray Cruises.
mechanism: Residential ship schemes remain ordinary consumer contracts under national law, so buyers' protection depends on a company's solvency and on courts on land.

name: Villa Vie Odyssey
pop: Company claims hundreds of full-time residents
challenge: No state challenge found; held up by repairs
cost: Cabins from $99,999 in 2024, plus monthly fees; from $129,999 by 2025
story: Villa Vie Residences bought Fred Olsen's former cruise ship Braemar and sold cabins, called villas, for $99,999 and up plus a monthly fee, for the working life of the vessel, at least 15 years. The maiden voyage was planned to reach 425 ports in 147 countries. Marketing was aimed at adventurous retirees and digital nomads. In summer 2024 the ship sat for months at the Harland & Wolff repair yard in Belfast, Northern Ireland, as the company worked on rudder shafts, steel and engines. A marketing manager said the firm had been humbled by what it takes to bring back a 30-year-old vessel after a four-year layup. It finally sailed on 30 September 2024. A company press release a year later claimed 46 countries, 138 ports and hundreds of full-time residents, with ownership from $129,999 and a 'Golden Passport' lifetime plan from $99,999. That passport is only a marketing name for a cruise plan and is not travel paper of any state. No sovereignty claim by the company was found.
mechanism: A residential ship offers a home outside any one country's daily reach, while still depending on a flag, repair yards and port states for permission to operate.

name: MS The World
founder: Knut Kloster; operated by ROW Management
pop: 150 to 200 passengers on average, with 280 crew
laws: Bahamas registry; Nassau is its port of registry
challenge: Never tested; it operates as a registered ship
story: MS The World is a private ship run like a condominium block, with large apartments that people buy. It was the idea of Knut Kloster, was first announced as The World of ResidenSea, was ordered in 2000, and was completed on 20 February 2002. Its port of registry is Nassau in the Bahamas, and it is operated from Fort Lauderdale, Florida, by ROW Management. Port of registry means the country whose flag the ship flies and whose law applies on board at sea. Residents come from many countries. Some live on board full-time and others visit periodically. On average it carries 150 to 200 passengers with a crew of 280. The encyclopedia entry on Freedom Ship names this project as the conservative counterpart, keeping to normal shipbuilding limits in place of building a mobile city. It makes no claim to statehood, and it is included as a working example of the ordinary legal route: a registered ship, a flag state and a private ownership agreement. The map marker shows Nassau, where it is registered, since the ship itself keeps moving.
mechanism: The World shows that people can live permanently at sea with no sovereignty claim, under an ordinary flag-state registration used as the legal base.

name: Oceanix Busan
founder: OCEANIX with UN-Habitat and Busan Metropolitan City
challenge: Not applicable; a state-backed project
recognition: Backed by UN-Habitat and Busan city; no independence claimed
story: On 26 April 2022, at UN Headquarters in New York, UN-Habitat, the city of Busan in South Korea and the company OCEANIX unveiled the design for what they called the world's first prototype sustainable floating city. The design came with a stated aim of giving coastal cities new land as seas rise and housing costs grow. UN-Habitat, the UN agency for cities, said two of every five people live within 100 kilometres of a coast and that 90 percent of mega cities are vulnerable to rising seas. The project matters to this map because of how it differs from the earlier seasteads. It sits inside national waters, is sponsored by a city government and has UN backing. It uses the same basic idea of floating land, with no attempt to leave any state's law. At the launch the partners said they were on track to deliver it. This research found no verified report of construction or residents, so it is listed as not yet built.
mechanism: Oceanix moves floating-city engineering inside a state's jurisdiction with UN support, separating the technical idea of building on the sea from the legal idea of leaving national law.

name: Women on Waves
stopped_by: Blocked at times by Portuguese warships and the Guatemalan army
laws: Dutch law applies on board, under a Dutch Ministry of Health permit
challenge: Yes. European Court of Human Rights found Portugal's 2004 blockade breached free expression
recognition: Not a sovereignty claim; uses Dutch flag-state law
story: Women on Waves is a Dutch group that sails to countries with restrictive abortion laws and takes women 12 miles offshore to international waters to give them abortion pills. National criminal law generally stops at the 12-mile territorial sea. Beyond it, on the high seas, the law of the ship's flag state applies. Its ship is registered in the Netherlands and holds a Dutch Ministry of Health permit. Its first voyage, to Ireland in 2001, was cut short for lack of a proper Dutch licence. In 2004 two Portuguese warships blocked its ship Borndiep from reaching Figueira da Foz. In February 2009 the European Court of Human Rights ruled that Portugal had breached freedom of expression and assembly, and that it could have used lighter steps such as seizing the pills. The group has also sailed to Poland, Spain, Morocco, Guatemala and Mexico. In Guatemala the army blocked the pier within 24 hours of docking. A law journal article notes that coastal states may still argue other grounds for jurisdiction. The most recent ship campaign found in these sources is Mexico.
mechanism: A ship registered in one state can carry that state's law onto the high seas, and Women on Waves v Portugal (2009) limited a coastal state's right to keep such a ship out.

name: Sea Shepherd and the piracy ruling
aka: Institute of Cetacean Research v. Sea Shepherd
stopped_by: US Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit reversed in the whalers' favour
challenge: Lost in the US appeal court, which called its acts piracy
story: Sea Shepherd Conservation Society, founded by Paul Watson in 1977, uses ships to confront whalers. Japanese researchers hunted whales in the Southern Ocean under a research permit issued by Japan, and sued Sea Shepherd in the United States under the Alien Tort Statute, a law letting foreigners bring certain claims in US courts. The trial court denied a preliminary injunction and dismissed the piracy claim. On 25 February 2013 the Ninth Circuit reversed. Chief Judge Kozinski wrote: 'You don't need a peg leg or an eye patch.' He listed ramming ships, throwing glass containers of acid, dragging metal-reinforced ropes to damage propellers, smoke bombs and flares with hooks, and pointing high-powered lasers at other ships. The UN Convention on the Law of the Sea defines piracy as illegal violence on the high seas committed for private ends by the crew of a private ship against another ship. The trial court had limited 'private ends' to financial enrichment. The appeal court said 'private' is normally the opposite of 'public' and is far broader than money. The case is included because it marks a limit on what private vessels can do on the high seas.
mechanism: The Ninth Circuit's 2013 Sea Shepherd ruling read 'private ends' in the piracy definition to cover goals beyond money, so activist attacks by private ships on the high seas can count as piracy.

name: SS Rex and the Santa Monica gambling ships
stopped_by: California Attorney General Earl Warren
pop: 1,000 to 3,000 gamblers aboard at any one time
challenge: Won on appeal over the bay question; lost to Warren's 1939 nuisance raids
story: From 1928, gambling ships anchored off Los Angeles County just past the 3-mile limit. Gambling was illegal in California, but the state's reach stopped there and federal law did not forbid it. Tony Cornero launched the SS Rex in 1938, running day and night with 1,000 to 3,000 gamblers aboard. District Attorney Buron Fitts arrested Cornero and argued that Santa Monica Bay was an inland bay, so the limit should be measured from a line between Point Vicente and Point Dume, which would push the ship much farther out. Cornero answered that it was a bight, an open curve in the coast. Fitts won at first, and the ruling was overturned on appeal. In 1939 Attorney General Earl Warren argued that a state could stop a nuisance even outside its jurisdiction. On 1 August 1939 authorities raided four ships. The Rex, which had no engines, blocked its landing platform and turned fire hoses on police boats. Cornero surrendered after eight days, saying he needed a haircut. A later court ruling closed the ships for good. In 1948 President Truman signed a federal ban on gambling ships in US waters.
mechanism: The fight tested where a baseline runs across a bay and whether a state can suppress a 'nuisance' beyond its limit, and federal law later closed the gap.

name: New Atlantis
stopped_by: Tropical storms
pop: Six people listed in 1965, including the Hemingway family
currency: The scruple, consisting of fish hooks, carob beans, shark teeth and similar items
laws: Constitution copied almost word for word from the US Constitution
challenge: No state acted; storms destroyed it
recognition: None. A State Department letter to the 'Acting President' was claimed as recognition. The Universal Postal Union refused its stamps
story: Leicester Hemingway, brother of Ernest, built a raft of bamboo, steel, iron pipe and rock, 8 by 30 feet, and had it towed about 6 to 8 miles off Bluefields, Jamaica, onto a shallow bank. He anchored it with an old Ford engine block, in waters then considered international. Its stated location was 18 degrees 1 minute north, 78 degrees 4 minutes west. On 4 July 1964 he declared a republic. (One profile gives 1965.) He claimed the raft under the US Guano Islands Act of 1856, which lets citizens claim guano-covered islands for the United States. He ceded the half where birds were encouraged to leave droppings to the US and kept the rest as his nation. By 1965 six people were listed as inhabitants, and they unanimously elected him president. He also claimed the seafloor 50 feet below and planned to pile up rocks into an island. He wanted to fund marine research by selling stamps, but the Universal Postal Union refused them. Within a few years tropical storms destroyed the raft, and local fishermen salvaged the wreckage.
mechanism: Hemingway's claim stretched the 1856 Guano Islands Act to a man-made raft, a theory never tried in court because storms ended the raft first.

name: Autopia
stopped_by: Lack of funds
challenge: Not tested; site lies beyond national jurisdiction
story: The Saya de Malha Bank is a huge submerged plateau in the Indian Ocean, less than 33 feet deep in places and hundreds of miles from any state's jurisdiction, according to reporter Ian Urbina. On 9 March 1997 architect Wolf Hilbertz and marine biologist Thomas Goreau sailed three days from Victoria in the Seychelles with solar panels, metal scaffolding and cornerstones. They meant to start a micronation called Autopia, 'the place that builds itself'. Hilbertz said most of the bank lay on the high seas, governed only by the UN Law of the Sea. In 2002 they came back in three sailboats with architects, cartographers and marine biologists. With a cyclone approaching, they built a steel frame five by five metres and two metres high in six days at 9 degrees 12 minutes south, 61 degrees 21 minutes east. The frame ran on a small battery. A process Hilbertz patented, Biorock, uses a weak electric current to deposit limestone on sunken steel, which he hoped to use for homes. He wanted a self-sufficient settlement belonging to its residents. The plans stalled for lack of money.
mechanism: Autopia tried a mid-ocean bank reported as beyond any nation's jurisdiction, where the obstacles were money and engineering and no state acted.

name: Aisland
stopped_by: A wave broke the barge on 2 February 2024; three people died
pop: Landi and a few crew: three sailors and a cook, by one account
challenge: Not challenged by a state
cost: Plan for about twenty barges by 2028; cost not verified
story: Samuele Landi was an Italian businessman whose company Eutelia went bankrupt in 2010. He was tried in Italy and sentenced in his absence to 14 years, and moved to Dubai. Urbina's reporting says he obtained Liberian diplomatic credentials, according to a New York Times profile. He bought an 800-ton deck barge, the Aisland, and anchored it about 30 miles off Dubai, with six shipping containers bolted to the deck as living quarters, solar air conditioning and a desalination unit. He lived there for over a year with three sailors, a cook and five cats, raising money for a larger barge to take to the Saya de Malha Bank in the Indian Ocean. He hoped for about twenty barges and thousands of residents by 2028, and planned to mount a Gatling gun against pirates. The Seasteading Institute says a captain warned him the barge was unsafe. On 2 February 2024 a wave broke the barge in two. Two crew survived, clinging to wood. Landi and two employees, named as Abdul and Javed Khan, died. His body came ashore about 40 miles up the coast.
mechanism: Landi's plan used distance from land to avoid extradition, and the structure's safety was left to him alone, with no flag state or classification society shown in these sources.

name: Deepsea Ventures seabed claim
aka: Notice of Discovery and Claim of Exclusive Mining Rights
challenge: Filed as a private claim; no court ruling was found
cost: 60,000 square kilometre tract; commercial production planned within 15 years
story: On 15 November 1974 Deepsea Ventures Inc. of Gloucester Point, Virginia, filed what Reason magazine called the world's first ocean mining claim. Its president, John Flipse, sent a 'Notice of Discovery and Claim of Exclusive Mining Rights, and Request for Diplomatic Protection and Protection of Investment' to Secretary of State Henry Kissinger and recorded a copy at the Gloucester County Circuit Court. Copies went by registered mail to cabinet members, congressional committees, ambassadors of maritime countries, oceanographers and other companies. The claim covered a 60,000-square-kilometre deposit of manganese nodules, which are potato-sized lumps of metal on the ocean floor, in the northeastern Pacific. It said the tract lay beyond the seabed jurisdiction of any state. The company promised commercial production within 15 years, running for 40 years. It asserted exclusive rights to mine and sell the nodules, and it stated that it did not assert a territorial claim or ask the US to make one. The map marker is an estimate, because the tract's coordinates were not in the page retrieved. This research found no sign that mining took place under the claim.
mechanism: Deepsea Ventures tried to create private property in seabed minerals by discovery and notice, separating resource rights from any claim to territory, before the Law of the Sea treaty assigned the area to an international authority.

name: International Seabed Authority regime
founder: UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (1982) and 1994 Implementation Agreement
laws: Mining code for exploitation still unfinished in 2026
challenge: In force; the US is not a member and has opened its own permit route
recognition: 171 member states plus the European Union
story: The International Seabed Authority is an intergovernmental body based in Kingston, Jamaica, set up on 16 November 1994 under the 1982 UN Convention on the Law of the Sea and a 1994 implementation agreement. It has 171 member states plus the European Union, and oversees the deep seabed outside national jurisdiction, covering about half of the world's ocean area. No person or state can own that seabed by simply claiming it, so private mining has to go through a contract with the authority, backed by a sponsoring member state. Since 1994 it has approved more than two dozen exploration contracts in the Atlantic, Pacific and Indian Oceans, most in the Clarion-Clipperton Zone between Hawaii and Mexico. It has not approved commercial mining. Its council met from 9 to 19 March 2026 without finishing its long-delayed mining code, with benefit-sharing, liability and environmental compensation unresolved. It continued an inquiry into whether contractors had breached obligations by seeking US permits. The United States has not ratified the treaty and is not a member.
mechanism: The seabed beyond national jurisdiction is governed as an international regime, so sponsorship by a member state and a contract with the authority replace claims by discovery or occupation.

name: The Metals Company and the US permit route
founder: DeepGreen Metals; Gerard Barron CEO from 2017
challenge: Under challenge: ISA inquiry now before the Seabed Disputes Chamber; NOAA decision pending
recognition: ISA contracts via Nauru and Tonga; US applications under national law
cost: DeepGreen merged with a listed shell company in a $2.9 billion deal in 2021
story: DeepGreen Metals was founded in 2011. That year the International Seabed Authority granted exploration contracts in the Clarion-Clipperton Zone, about 1,500 miles southwest of San Diego, to Nauru Ocean Resources (NORI), sponsored by Nauru, and Tonga Offshore Mining (TOML), sponsored by Tonga. The company owned NORI and later bought TOML. It went public as The Metals Company in 2021. That June, Nauru told the authority it meant to begin mining, which triggered a two-year deadline to finish rules. On 24 April 2025 President Trump signed an order telling the US ocean agency NOAA to speed permits under a US law, the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act. Four days later the company's US arm applied for licences and a commercial recovery permit. It filed a consolidated application covering about 65,000 square kilometres on 22 January 2026, and NOAA found it fully compliant on 28 April, which the company's filing says is not an approval. The authority opened an inquiry into NORI and TOML, which is now before the Seabed Disputes Chamber of the international law of the sea tribunal, and it extended NORI's contract to 21 July 2031.
mechanism: The company is testing whether a firm can mine the international seabed under one country's national permit, outside the treaty regime that its own subsidiaries hold contracts under.

name: Dominion of Melchizedek
founder: Mark Pedley, possibly with his father David Pedley
stopped_by: Marshall Islands condemned it; people tied to it were convicted of crimes
passports: Sold widely; regarded as fraudulent. A 1998 Philippine scheme grossed about US$1 million
challenge: Never held territory to defend. People linked to it were convicted of fraud
recognition: Central African Republic reportedly in 1993, per the Washington Post; otherwise none
cost: One source estimates over US$500 million raised across schemes
story: The Dominion of Melchizedek was declared in 1990 by American Mark Pedley, whose father David had been convicted of financial crimes in the 1970s. It had no fixed home. It first claimed Malpelo, a Colombian island, then a place called Karitane Shoal in the South Pacific, supposedly under water for part of the day, which appears to have been invented. It also claimed Clipperton Island, a French possession, and Taongi or Bokak Atoll in the Marshall Islands. The Dallas Observer reported its spokesman describing Karitane as 14 square miles of sandy beaches. Marshall Islands Circular Note 01-98, of 23 April 1998, condemned its claims as fraudulent. The group's use was financial. In 1991 shell banks in Washington, D.C., tried to get loans using fake Melchizedek securities and were shut down. Passports sold for up to $3,500. Three people posing as officials were arrested in the Philippines in 1998. One source puts total sums raised above US$500 million. Its representatives were also banned from Rotuma, a Fijian island, after dealing with groups seeking to secede from Fiji.
mechanism: The case shows a sovereignty claim used to sell passports and financial paper, with claims to reefs and shoals and no occupation behind them.

name: Kingdom of EnenKio
stopped_by: US Securities and Exchange Commission; Marshall Islands government
laws: Moore styled himself Minister Plenipotentiary
challenge: No. Assets frozen by a US federal judge in October 2000
recognition: None; Marshall Islands issued a formal denial
cost: $1 billion bond offering marketed online
story: Wake Island is a remote Pacific atoll controlled by the United States since 1899 and claimed by the Marshall Islands as Ānen Kio. In 1994 Honolulu resident Robert F. Moore, saying he acted for a Marshallese chief, Murjel Hermios, announced that the US had been given the boot and that an independent kingdom existed. It issued passports. In 1997 the Marshall Islands Journal reported that the kingdom had declared war on the United States and was asking for Marshallese support. On 23 April 1998 the Marshall Islands government issued Circular Note 01-98, condemning its claims and Melchizedek's, and saying the representatives were not citizens and had no right to speak for Marshallese landowners. In October 2000 the US Securities and Exchange Commission won a restraining order from Judge Susan Mollway in Honolulu. Moore had marketed $1 billion in 'Enenkio Gold War Bonds' online, saying they were backed by gold and promising 10 percent compound interest after five years. The SEC said no gold or other backing existed and the bonds were unregistered. The order froze his assets and required him to account for the money.
mechanism: A claimed sovereign's bond sale was stopped under ordinary US securities law, and a real government's written denial removed the story of local authority behind it.

name: Oceania / The Atlantis Project
stopped_by: Lack of funds and interest
laws: A complete constitution and system of laws were written in advance
challenge: Not tested
cost: About $1 billion estimated to start construction
story: Eric Klien began the Atlantis Project in February 1993 after he said a Libertarian candidate, Tamara Clark, lost a Nevada state senate race through election fraud. Its goal was a new country called Oceania, built from about 80 hexagon units at first, for 10,000 to 30,000 people. The project's own online FAQ priced the start at roughly one billion dollars and placed the site about fifty miles northeast of the coast of Panama, on water it described as 100 feet deep, near trade routes, in an area it said had no recorded hurricanes. It published a full constitution and legal code before anything was built, under the slogan 'Break the Chains'. Klien later told VICE that the main reason it failed was too little interest, and that communicating before the web was costly, through phones and newspaper ads. Promotion ran largely through mailing lists and a Usenet group. Klien went on to run the Lifeboat Foundation. A site 50 miles off Panama sits inside the 200-mile exclusive economic zone that the Law of the Sea treaty gives coastal states, which the project never had to confront.
mechanism: Oceania relied on being outside the 12-mile limit, though its site lay within Panama's 200-mile resource zone, a conflict never tested because nothing was built.

name: Aquarius Reef Base
founder: US government and university programme; operated by Florida International University
pop: Small research crews for days at a time
laws: US federal waters rules; sits in the Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary
challenge: Never challenged; a state-sanctioned lab
recognition: Not a claim; US research facility
story: Aquarius is an underwater laboratory on the sea floor 62 feet down, next to Conch Reef, 5.4 miles off Key Largo, Florida. It lies in the Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary and is operated by Florida International University. Crews use saturation diving: after staying under pressure their bodies reach a steady state, so they can work outside for up to nine hours a day and only decompress at the end. Research has ranged from coral disease to nutrient cycling. NASA uses it to train astronauts for spacewalks and lunar missions. Encyclopedia sources give 1986 as the date the programme was established. Until 2026, reporters described it as the only undersea research laboratory in operation. It is included as the working baseline for undersea living. Unlike the micronations on this map, people live there for days without making any claim of independence, and the habitat is part of a US government-managed marine area. It has never been the basis for any claim to the seabed below it.
mechanism: Aquarius shows the usual arrangement for undersea habitats: placed in a coastal state's managed waters, run under its authority, with no claim to the seabed.

name: DEEP Vanguard and Sentinel
pop: Three people for up to a week in Vanguard, by design; six per Sentinel module planned
laws: Sited in US waters off Florida; no independence claim
challenge: Not challenged
story: DEEP is a UK-based private company building undersea habitats. Its prototype, Vanguard, was installed in the Florida Keys in June 2026, according to the Miami Herald via WLRN. That made it the Keys' second undersea habitat and a privately funded one. The company's director of scientific research, Dawn Kernagis, said it had been over 40 years since a new human undersea habitat was launched. Vanguard is designed for three people at depths of 100 metres for up to a week. It is the first step toward a larger system called Sentinel, planned for 2027. Sentinel's modules would hold six people each, join into a larger complex, and let people stay at 200 metres for 28 days, on the continental shelf. Boat International reported it might go to the Mediterranean. The modules can be moved, reconfigured and redeployed, a feature that raises the question of which state controls them at each site. DEEP makes no sovereignty claim. Coverage found for this research describes science and industry uses, and reports nothing about seeking independence from the country where a habitat sits.
mechanism: Private undersea habitats on the continental shelf fall within a coastal state's rights over that shelf, so moving a module means moving to a different state's permission.

name: Proteus
laws: Planned for a marine area off Curaçao
challenge: Not applicable
story: Proteus is an undersea research station proposed by Fabien Cousteau, grandson of the explorer Jacques Cousteau, through his company Proteus Ocean Group. As of an October 2024 Boat International report it was still in planning, with launch hoped for around 2027 and heavy funding still needed. It would sit in Curaçao, at a depth of about 20 metres, with a deeper satellite module at 70 metres. Like DEEP's Sentinel it is modular, and could expand to hold up to 18 people. Both projects target the sunlit zone of the ocean, home to about 90 percent of marine species. An expert quoted in that report said going under water is very costly and has been harder to achieve than reaching the moon. The Spanish tech site Xataka reported that only four undersea habitats were running worldwide at the time. Proteus would sit within a named state's waters, near the Caribbean island of Curaçao. It first reached the press in August 2020, the start year used here. No claim of sovereignty over the seabed or the water above was found.
mechanism: Proteus would be built inside a specific island's waters by agreement, the common legal pattern for undersea stations, with no attempt to create new jurisdiction.

name: Ocean Spiral
challenge: Not applicable
cost: ¥3 trillion (US$25 billion) estimated for construction
story: In November 2014 Japanese construction company Shimizu Corporation published a design for an underwater city called Ocean Spiral, reported in the trade press with a 'Blue Garden' core. The plan described a 75-storey colony housing 5,000 people in linked spheres, with over 1,000 homes, a 400-room hotel and 50,000 square metres of offices. Each watertight sphere would be attached to the ocean floor and could sink below the surface in bad weather. Power would come from micro-organism factories producing methane, and drinking water from desalination. Shimizu expected the needed technology by 2030, and then five more years of building, at a cost of ¥3 trillion, about US$25 billion. It expected Japan's government and private investors to help pay. This is an example of the undersea-city type of proposal, presented as a corporate concept for a state and investors to fund. The design says nothing about leaving any national law. It names no site in the sources found, so the map marker is placed in Japan, the company's home country, as a placeholder.
mechanism: Ocean Spiral assumes government funding and sits outside the sovereignty argument, showing that undersea-city schemes need not imply leaving state jurisdiction.
